often used to study the cause-and-effect relationship of shock compression and thermal instability in the solar wind's formation of dense structures. Using a kinetic fluid model, we investigated the growth of thermal instability in the downstream area of a bow shock, located at the heliosphere's boundary, at different magnetic field angles. The results show that the magnetic field can hinder the development of thermal instability in the shock's downstream area, especially in the case of a perpendicular magnetic field, which significantly suppresses the instability. For shock angles above 45°, the magnetic field's influence becomes negligible at high magnetic strengths. For lower-angle shocks, however, the magnetic field can have its full effect, with growth rates decreasing linearly with increasing magnetic strength. For shock angles below 45°, the presence of significant seed turbulence near the heliosphere's boundary would likely cause magnetic reconnection in the shock's downstream area, leading to particle heating and enhanced thermal instability. Our analysis, encompassing various shock and magnetic field configurations, offers a comprehensive model that can be tested against actual heliospheric observations, aiding in the verification of thermal instability's role in the formation of shock-derived dense structures, particularly those with large magnetic fields.

, known as the Outer Automaton problem, involves determining whether a given $n$-ary permutation function can be realized as a component of a cycle within a multi-cycle complex system. This function serves as an input for the computational process and has historically led researchers to explore various specialized problems stemming from this core query such as determining the decomposability of specific functions. This paper presents a novel approach for solving the Outer Automaton problem by representing the permutation function using circuits comprising binary gates and efficiently verifying certain properties associated with its computational path. Unlike previous outcomes where no polynomial-time solution was possible, our method offers a distinct computational pathway where the involved function can be processed through an efficient circuit and its properties analyzed in a time-complexity matching $O(n\log^2n)$. Consequently, we conclude that the decision process associated with the Outer Automaton problem can be resolved within the computational $NP$ category. Furthermore, we draw a parallel between this finding and a previously reported $NP$ resolution for determining the decomposability of binary functions through a similar algorithmic process with matching time-complexity $O(n\log^2n)$. Our methods offer substantial improvements to the computational efficiency of resolving these complex queries compared to the previously reported methods of Bacher-Lin and others.

few-shot learning is an essential capability for artificial intelligence. However, traditional methods often struggle with the limited data by overfitting to the trained classes. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes a prior knowledge base to enhance few-shot learning. We call this method 'Few-shot Factual Networks' (FFNs), a data-friendly neural framework that integrates prior knowledge in a unsupervised manner. FFNs contains a knowledge module, consisting of pairwise knowledge graphs and a knowledge embedding network, which dynamically and adaptably injects auxiliary knowledge into the network. We demonstrate that this approach allows FFNs to effectively utilize external knowledge while maintaining compatibility with existing unsupervised relation embedding methods. We conducted comprehensive experiments on 1-shot and 5-shot classification tasks with support sets of size 1 and 5. Our results show that FFNs surpasses state-of-the-art methods and exhibits impressive robustness and data efficiency.

Inverse Compton scattering, where relativistic electrons upshift radiation from lower frequencies, is essential for producing radio emission. The polarization degree of this scattered radiation depends on the local electron distribution. Research has shown that the electron distribution can be determined by analyzing the polarization degree as a function of frequency in radio sources. This study investigates how the electron distribution function affects the radio polarization degree in sources radioted by an AGN, assuming the radio spectrum exhibits a single power law. Assuming a general electron distribution function, the calculated polarization degree differs significantly from that predicted by a standard relativistic Maxwellian electron distribution with an index $p=3.4$ for sources with a harder spectrum and $p=2.5$ for those with a softer spectrum. The amplitude of the electron distribution function also influences the polarization degree. Notably, the polarization degree remains unchanged for sources with an index $p=3$ across all spectral configurations. This research lays the groundwork for a theoretical analysis how the electron distribution function is determined in radio sources through observing the polarization degree as a function of frequency.

3D point cloud-based place recognition excels in areas lacking GPS functionality and serves a pivotal role in map-based navigation systems. Traditional place recognition excels in environments with duplicate places but struggles with diverse scene variations. Recent advancements in deep learning have boosted place recognition performance, yet these approaches primarily focus on 2D projections and disregard 3D geometry information when processing variants. To adequately tackle diverse scene variations and exhaustive 3D geometry detailing, this research proposes a innovative pipeline combining place recognition and a generative model. It initially extracts robust and efficient place descriptors from 3D point clouds, combined with 2D and 3D depth maps, via a multi-modal network. Subsequently, a conditioned diffusion model generates descriptive and comprehensive 3D geometry descriptors to address diverse scene variations. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in comparing with state-of-the-art place recognition methods.

higher-dimensional equivalent, known as the Tug-of-War, are key concepts that have been extensively studied within graph theory. By extending these ideas to graphs, we aim to solve a similar problem within a more general mathematical framework. This study introduces the concept of harmonic morphisms, which generalize the notion of minimum weight spanning trees, to solve the Spanning Tree Problem. A spanner, which is a generalization ofug-of-War, satisfies specific conditions and provides an alternative solution to the Spanning Tree Problem. A key finding of this study demonstrates that every connected graph has an integer spanner with the minimum possible diameter, which solves the Spanning Tree Problem. This result enables the solution of any instance of the Spanning Tree Problem within polynomial time. Additionally, this study establishes a direct correlation between the minimum weight spanning tree, the Tug-of-War, and spanners, which offers new perspectives on the relationship between graph theory and their corresponding generalized concepts. Furthermore, a significant outcome of this study proves that any given graph has a spanner, which serves as both the minimum weight spanning tree and the Tug-of-War simultaneously.

Our primary focus is on mitigating these vulnerabilities and enhancing the robustness of GNN models. To do this, we must first understand the nature of GNN vulnerabilities. Our analysis encompasses four key aspects: (1) the types of inputs that can trigger vulnerabilities, (2) the specific models that can be affected, (3) the features that can be targeted, and (4) the types of attacks that can be performed. Our findings suggest that GNN vulnerabilities are influenced by multiple factors such as the type of attack, data representation, graph structure, and neural network architecture. To address these vulnerabilities, we propose four novel strategies for GNN defensive distillation: (1) the use of multiple robust input representation schemes in adversarial training, (2) the use of graph filter augmentation in feature-wise adversarial training, (3) the use of multi-head discriminator augmentation in graph structure-aware adversarial training, and (4) the use of graph filter and node feature perturbation augmentation in graph structure-aware adversarial training. Our experiments on semi-supervised node classification tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed defenses in mitigating various GNN vulnerabilities.

Using these methods, the research demonstrates how to calculate a unified measure of sensitivity that is applicable to both fixed and variable low precision programs that dynamically change their accuracy levels.

Notably, our results show that the models have little impact on cross sections but different starting points in Born terms lead to significant differences in cross sections, especially in the isospin-3/2 channel where the photon nucleon system has resonances, and the effects are most pronounced at higher spin resonances like N(2) and Delta(2). Additionally, we examined the effects of including high-spin resonances in the models by using two types of channels: one with small-spin channels only and another that also includes high-spin channels like N(2) and Delta(2). Our results show that the resonance characteristics in the latter case are significantly affected by the inclusion of high-spin resonances.

Sketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors from a high-dimensional to a low-dimensional space. CountSketch achieves this by first incorporating random sign changes into the input vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, resulting in a vector $s \odot x$, where $s \in \{-1, 1\}^d$. The resulting vector is then aggregated into $k \ll d$ values by calculating the sum of entries within each of the $k$ buckets. Finally, the inner products between any pair of vectors can be estimated by repeating this process multiple times. Although researchers previously demonstrated that the optimal sketch for inner product estimation involves quadratic measurements, in this paper, it is demonstrated that CountSketch, which only contains a linear term, performs optimally when the inputs are drawn from a Gaussian distribution and further generates an information-theoretic lower bound for the problem.

This thermal equilibrium state is characterized by specific properties of the variables $u$ and $v$, which represent velocity and energy balance, respectively. we studied a distant spiral galaxy at a redshift of 2.773, called MZ, with significant star formation occurring along its disk, at a rate of approximately 0.05 solar masses per year per year per square kiloparsec. Our findings indicate that gas is being consumed from the disk, while stellar growth has now become negligible due to the consumption of gas. We hypothesize that MZ's star formation is being suppressed by feedback from stellar and black hole radiation and radiation pressure from stars. Moreover, we discovered that MZ's spiral arms, which once supported its star formation, have been stripped of gas, forcing the galaxy to rely on gas accretion from outside sources. We conclude that MZ, with its spiral structure and ongoing star formation despite external gas accretion, serves as a valuable insight into how similar galaxies function during the early stages of cosmic history.

is designed to explore the potential of optical optical clocks, combining synchronization, time-stamping, and feedback mechanisms to maintain two clocks within a specific frequency range over distances. Potential uses include calibrating devices, enhancing GPS, enabling precise device comparisons, and improving geodesy measures across greater distances. To bring these applications to life, we need to overcome significant hurdles, such as achieving high levels of accuracy while using available technology and overcoming potential disruptions caused by atmospheric interference and potential network failures. To improve efficiency, CMSICNet employs a low-computation residual learning approach that reduces computation requirements. To preserve detailed image representation, it uses normal cross entropy loss in the final stage and high-frequency reconstruction loss across earlier stages. We conducted a study to assess how end-users perceive these explanations and their impact on building trust in AI systems.

We observed adaptive synchronization in a collective of agents, or entities.
This collective exhibits a dynamic, adaptable coupling between pairs of agents, leading to complex entangled behaviors, rather than following standard coupled cluster synchronization patterns.
In cases where adaptability has a short memory or where the agents' desired state exhibits weak non-linearity, we identified two distinct zones that support adaptive synchronization: the strong non-linear range and a region of weak non-linearity characterized by exponential non-binomial distributions of entrainment outcomes.

This problem has been efficiently solved for planar graphs with fixed $r$, but remains computationally difficult when the graph's planar property is replaced by having bounded genus. To overcome this challenge, our work presents a new approach that achieves near-optimal results by exploiting the approximate multiplicative structure of small distance-dominating sets to derive a parameterization based on both the graph's genus and its number of vertices. This approach yields an $O(\gamma \cdot \log \gamma \cdot n)$-approximation algorithm that can be computed in time $g^{O(\sqrt{\log g})}(\gamma \cdot \kappa + n)\cdot \text{poly}(\sqrt{r})$, where $g$ denotes the genus of the surface on which the graph resides, $n$ is the number of vertices in the graph, and each vertex in the graph is within a distance of $r$ from at least one vertex in $D$. This approach significantly surpasses the previously achieved $O(n \cdot \log g)$-approximation algorithms for planar graphs.

the Andromeda galaxy has been created using archival data from the International Ultraviolet Explorer satellite. "Werewolf," is a social deduction game that focuses on social deception and discernment through interactions that reveal concealed information. Research has been conducted to analyze this phenomenon both in human psychology and in artificial intelligence contexts. However, the complexity of the game lies in the fact that all participants have hidden motives and secret identities. Both inaccurate information sharing and strategic responses are essential aspects of achieving success in the game. While there have been various implementations of these games for analysis, they have often relied on simplified algorithms such as the K-nearest neighbor classifier, Backpropagation neural networks, or A* heuristic for bots, whereas humans typically excel in data analysis but may struggle in other areas. In this study, a novel approach for analyzing the game dynamics is explored that utilizes a dynamic network model where all participants have hidden identities and secret motives.

Unfortunately, current load shedding approaches often neglect to consider security requirements while implementing prioritization, which can result in unintended security consequences. To resolve this issue, this research introduces load shedding in service-oriented computing as an optimization problem that simultaneously considers load, quality and security metrics. By developing an overhead-aware QoS-quality and security-based load shedding algorithm, we achieve simultaneous satisfaction of prioritization and load shedding objectives. We also observe that the circular cylinder is a particular instance of a torus. We investigate how the circular cylinder and torus topologies relate to one another in terms of their burstonian moduli spaces and observe that their difference lies in merely adding two discrete options for the burston bundle's class. We demonstrate that the torus's two types of moduli affect the form factors by introducing distinct quasiperiodic phases during their horizontal and vertical shifts, respectively. oplanetary disks is a common observation, but the origins of these observations remain uncertain.  Disk observations reveal features on diverse spatial scales spanning a wide range of time periods, indicating the existence of multiple disk formation mechanisms.  In this research, we investigate ring characteristics on a small spatial and long temporal scale by examining pre-main-sequence stars surrounded by dusty disks within the Taurus T Tauri Association.  Utilizing high-resolution submillimeter continuum images from the ALMA telescope, we identified four T Tauri stars showing sub-mm flux enhancements.  Our findings suggest that these associations represent transient phenomena occurring during the disk evolution process.  The existence of disk rings is likely temporary and occurs within a specific timeframe following the birth of a star.  This hypothesis aligns with the observed properties of the detected rings as well as the probability calculations considering the evolutionary stage of the central stars within the Taurus star-forming region.  The existence of rings suggests the presence of disk density variations occurring naturally due to viscous evolution rather than artificial processes like a passing star.

the irregularities in the big bang cosmological model are to an irregular background in space. It's established that in the framework of general relativity, a consistent, non-constant spatial background in the absence of a cosmological constant is impossible in an energy and momentum sourced environment. Therefore, we propose a slight modification to the Einstein field equations, introducing a non-constant background term that can accommodate initial irregularities in the big bang universe. Using a gauge that is natural to the proposed modification, we demonstrate that under a specific set of assumptions, long-term evolution in the universe leads to a gauge-invariant and smooth state, effectively isolating the true dynamics from the introduced background term. Furthermore, we show that our approach can make linearly growing metric perturbations consistent with the new framework. Finally, we extend the analysis to encompass quadratic and higher-order effects, concluding that our proposed approach can reconcile the initial conditions in the big bang universe with a consistent background in the framework of general relativity.

cycle of expansion and contraction is explored, with research on whether Newtonian dynamics can represent such phenomena. Studies of the Newtonian Universe's behavior have primarily relied on the overdensity matrix, with scientists investigating its eigenvalues to determine if the Newtonian framework can accommodate periodicity. Previous studies found periodic solutions but were limited by their reliance on high nonlinearity, which is unsuitable for describing the early Universe's behavior. This paper proposes the use of the eigenvalues of the overlap matrix, the linear counterpart of the overdensity matrix, and demonstrates, through both analytical and numerical methods, that it yields periodic solutions in both homogeneous and inhomogeneous fields. These analytical solutions, derived from the WKB method, can easily explain phenomena such as acoustic oscillations and matter clustering, and were previously challenging within the context of General Relativity.

the analysis of the Dirac operator's spectral profile reveals that its eigenvalues approach zero at a rate proportional to $N^{-1}$. However, this method often incorporates numerous extra quantum gates within each quantum circuit due to gate decomposition and is susceptible to disturbances caused by uncontrolled interactions. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel, effective technique to minimize noise by identifying and strategic removing quantum system eigenmodes that could be influenced by external noise. Initially, we modify the quantum circuit through the introduction of supplementary qubits to ensure eigenmode. Next, we calculate a corresponding anti-transformation that reverses the effect of the added qubits and removes unnecessary frequency components from the original quantum system, resulting in a version of the quantum circuit that is more resilient to external noise. We demonstrate the implementation of this technique through examples by applying it to Grover's and the Shor's algorithms.

We've theoretically modeled the properties of these interactions, which can occur on scales smaller than the system's governing geostrophic vortices. We considered two scenarios: one involving small-scale, two-dimensional eddies and another involving t, a scale at which the system transitions to unbalanced, three-dimensional flow. We've shown that t, known as the dissipative scale, marks the point at which balanced rotation interactions begin to form small, 3D, unbalanced Kolmogorov eddies that eventually dissipate. These super-geostrophic rotations are primarily responsible for developing balanced quasi-2D geostrophic vortices. We've confirmed our predictions using data from three-dimensional rotating turbulence simulations and experiments. These results are significant for understanding the dynamics of atmospheric and oceanic systems, as well as any similar situations where rapid rotation is involved, as they indicate that wave-cascade super-geostrophic rotations are a common feature of these systems.

Assistant, primarily utilize speech recognition and natural language processing to comprehend and respond to voice-based requests. Our research focuses on the impact of these two factors on voice assistant interactions, resulting in approximately 37% of requests requiring modification before being processed. Combining human assistance with existing assistant applications could potentially streamline interactions, minimize required modifications, and enhance user satisfaction with these systems.

Research has shown that satellite data can effectively contribute to wildfire detection, yet research has not been extensively conducted on combining data from multiple sources, including ground-based sensors. This paper presents an innovative neural network approach that fuses observations from satellites and other ground-based sensors to accurately locate and monitor wildfires. Our proposed approach, known as DeepDA, is a hierarchical, probabilistic framework that can work with limited labeled data. By leveraging the strength of unsupervised learning, DeepDA can automatically integrate diverse input data, minimizing the need for manual intervention. Through simulated and real-world data, we've demonstrated that DeepDA can successfully combine multi-modal observations to accurately map fire locations and boundaries. Our approach also allows us to quantify the uncertainty of each source's contribution, providing valuable decision-making support for wildfire monitoring and response.

A precise measurement of $R_\Sigma$ is proposed to provide more sensitive evidence for possible new physics effects in the $b\to s\gamma$ process. A possible source of systematics in $R_\Sigma$ measurement is identified in the relative acceptance of electron and muon detectors at $R_\Sigma$'s reconstruction.

The success of these models is largely dependent on finding an optimal balance between model complexity and performance when processing time is a consideration. The development of accurate and efficient models is particularly crucial when contrasting theoretical predictions with experimental data. In eco-evolutionary dynamics research, multiple modeling techniques have been employed to simplify complex systems by making assumptions that limit their applicability. To overcome this limitation, we have created an innovative modeling framework that uses a generalized version of the Fisher equation to model growth in a variety of eco-evolutionary systems, assesses model accuracy when complex model assumptions are removed, and identifies areas for potential improvement. The generalized Fisher equation is analyzed in a scenario where environmental changes are influenced by a moving wave pattern that affects growth and exponentiation in a uniform population. The model reveals that environmental modifications can lead to the emergence of multiple wave patterns and that this phenomenon is linked to a turning point in the system's behavior, known as a branch point in the solution set. The model's robustness is highlighted by its ability to accurately predict growth patterns in the absence of additional assumptions on population dynamics, utilizing merely the fundamental principles of environmental modification and population growth. The model's robustness is further validated by its performance in a scenario where localized environmental modifications are introduced into a moving wave pattern, demonstrating its accuracy when the typical assumptions of uniform growth patterns and unbounded growth rates in a population are removed.

To achieve this, we investigated how these techniques are implemented in the context of verified security protocols and computer-based demonstrations. By doing so, we were able to assess the effectiveness of various methods when dealing with non-logical aspects of computer science problems, a field that is still underexplored. To facilitate our analysis, we employed a range of Computer Science problems, including access control configuration checks, network security path verifications, database security verifications, configuration check simulations, network topology colorings, and more. Our findings show that while several logical approaches, such as Satisfiability Modulo Arithmetic and First-Order Logic with Equality, are suitable for verifiable security protocol analysis, they are ill-suited for comprehensive computer-based demonstrations and may not even adequately represent the underlying problem. In contrast, we discovered that SAT solving, although versatile, is computationally expensive and may not efficiently utilize available resources. To address this issue, we proposed a novel approach that leverages SAT solvers in a more direct and efficient manner, while also demonstrating the successful application of this method on realistic network topology colorings. Our research has broader implications, suggesting that there is a need to expand the existing framework of Automated Reasoning to accommodate non-logical computer science approaches, such as SAT solving, and to explore the underlying structure of these non-logical approaches.

itivity Analysis, offers an approach to evaluating the impact of changes in input data on analysis outcomes. This method serves as a versatile design feature that accommodates any kind of data analysis, facilitating uncertainty evaluation across diverse domains. In this research, we employ Sensitivity Analysis to investigate the effect of modifications in the National Election Pool tabulations on predictions regarding the 2020 US presidential election under the scenario of mail-in ballots being excluded in California, Michigan, and Wisconsin. The framework in this research involves leveraging a formal approach grounded in denotational semantics that utilizes partial functions to represent the degree of uncertainty in input data by incorporating partial functions for analyses and fusing functions to produce fused outputs from fused inputs. To assess the variations in the predictions as a result of alterations in the input data, we employ probabilistic models established by Bayesian inference. The findings reveal a high degree of uncertainty in the predictions for the state of Wisconsin, potentially leading to the conclusion that the state is effectively a tie.

technology enables more precise and efficient management of complex systems. The primary objective is to minimize energy consumption, reduce environmental impact, and increase operational performance in industrial settings. The synergy between industrial operations and the Internet of Things (IoTs) facilitates data collection, analysis, and decision-making for optimizing production processes and maintenance schedules. However, individual AI and IoT components alone may not suffice for solving complex, interconnected problems. A more comprehensive approach utilizing AI and IoT in conjunction with Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) and Edge Computing (EC) is required. The Internet of Cyber-Physical Systems (IoCPS) leverages a network of interconnected entities including sensors, robots, and Edge Computing capabilities to gather, analyze, and share data in real-time. The incorporation of Edge Computing enables swift and intelligent processing of data near its source, thereby minimizing latency and improving responsiveness. This research explores the concept of Internet of Cyber-Physical Systems (ICPS), also known as Internet of Cyber-Physical Systems, a convergence of IoT, AI, and Edge Computing. By combining AI and CPS functionalities with EC processing, ICPS enables seamless collaboration and synchronization of cyber, physical, and edge components for holistic system management. A comprehensive framework encompassing network architectures, components, and practical case studies is presented to demonstrate the practicality and potential applications of ICPS.

increasingly larger numbers of transistors in next-generation integrated circuits has prompted the need for innovative cooling solutions. Traditional air-based cooling methods have reached their limitations, and researchers are now investigating alternatives such as liquid cooling. The cooling performance of a liquid cooling system comprises two components: the effectiveness of the heat transfer process and the efficiency of the system's design to minimize thermal resistance. The cooling capacity of the system is heavily reliant on the liquid's thermal conductivity, which can be significantly improved by incorporating nanoparticles. Theoretical models have proven the potential of using nanoparticles to achieve the desired enhancement, and the effectiveness of nanoparticle-enhanced cooling is further validated through numerical simulations. The simulations reveal that a combination of specific nanoparticle shapes and arrangements can lead to a substantial increase in cooling capacity, with well-arranged cylindrical nanoparticles exhibiting a up to 10-fold improvement over well-arranged spherical nanoparticles. The simulations also highlight that nanoparticle arrangement plays a significant role in cooling capacity, with both effective and ineffective arrangements possible. The variability in cooling capacity is attributed to the nanoparticle's shape alone, with well-arranged nanoparticles showing increased cooling capacity compared to poorly-arranged counterparts. The simulations further indicate that nanoparticle arrangement can have a substantial impact on heat transfer, with well-arranged nanoparticles exhibiting up to 10-fold improvement over poorly-arranged counterparts.

Unlike conventional inverse scattering methods, our formulation incorporates a spatially varying wave equation, eliminating the necessity for a homogeneous Earth assumption typically required by Born inversion. To achieve this deconvolution, we introduce a new approach, Full Waveform Inverse Scattering (FWIS), which transforms the wave equation into a simplified form with a specific type of source term representing Earth's subsurface properties. This term can be determined by the wave equation's solution and the seismic data using standard Wave Equation Inversion (EWI) techniques. However,FWIS exhibits certain limitations, including the need for small step sizes leading to computational inefficiency and sensitivity to seismic data errors. To overcome these challenges, we combine EWI with FWIS, resulting in a unified method called Wave Equation Based Structural Imaging (WESI). Our study demonstrates that WESI exhibits improved sensitivity to seismic data and enables the recovery of subsurface structures with sharp boundaries, providing a valuable imaging technique for seismic imaging and subsurface exploration.

To overcome these limitations, an innovative sampling strategy is presented within the CoILaT approach to maximize the geometric contrast between pre-trained image and text embeddings. the medical field is expanding rapidly, yet many models are still evaluated in limited settings and performance assessments are based on basic metrics like accuracy and AUC that are inadequate for clinical settings. The diversity of image styles from different hospitals, clinical centers, and devices can cause significant performance variations, and patient sampling bias from single institutions can cause substantial discrepancies in machine learning results. To better account for these challenges in machine learning models used for medical image analysis, we have developed a new framework called TAME that focuses on modeling and mitigating domain shift issues using spectral graph theory. This new framework utilizes undirected graphs constructed using graph convolutional networks to block the flow of domain-specific features, and instead emphasize class-specific features. Additionally, we have developed statistics-based metrics such as spectral diversity and accuracy gaps to better assess and improve model performance across diverse patient populations and devices. Our approach has been tested on various MRI datasets including multi-site ADNI, TAME, and cardiac MRI with vendor differences, resulting in improved generalizability demonstrated through classification performance gains. Furthermore, our newly introduced metrics and analyses provide insights into the impact of patient sampling on model performance variability across diverse medical imaging settings.

Neural Networks (DCNNs), have significantly advanced the field of image classification. However, they are highly susceptible to small, carefully crafted adversarial inputs that can easily trick the models into making incorrect predictions. This research explores the use of DCNNs as a tool to detect such adversarial inputs through the development of an inverse activation layer. By incorporating this layer, classical DCNNs gain the ability to "draw" images without the constraints of traditional grid-like grid structures, allowing for the reconstruction of original adversarial inputs and enabling more accurate image classification. Our approach utilizes this image reconstruction to uncover previously undetected vulnerabilities in existing CNN architectures.

A graph is considered $S$-closed if any edge connecting a vertex in $S$ to a vertex outside of $S$ actually connects two vertices in $S$. The subset of a graph's vertices responsible for separating it into two open-ended infinite networks is known as the vertex cut. In this context, researchers are those working on graph theory who study the closing operation's impact on the vertex cut's existence in an infinite graph. A key issue in this domain is identifying the minimum size of the hole required to separate an infinite graph into two open-ended networks. This study reveals that removing the vertex cut from an infinite graph and closing it with respect to a cut-vertex results in a closed graph. This research also introduces the concept of minimal and maximal closing operation sizes in an infinite graph, showing that these values can vary between certain limits. The study defines the closing operation size of an infinite graph as an element of an unbounded set of natural numbers. This study also proves that any infinite graph can be transformed into another with a specific hole size by removing a certain vertex cut. This research opens up avenues for the study of the behavior of the closing operation on the structure of the vertex cut and its importance in understanding the structure of the vertex cut.

-19 is RT-PCR, but it comes with drawbacks: it can't detect active COVID-19, requires invasive swabbing procedures which may cause infections and discomfort, and is prone to false positives or negatives. To overcome these limitations, scientists have developed digital PCR, a more sensitive PCR method capable of quantifying target DNA in patient samples by partitioning the reaction into tiny units to avoid excessive amplification by background DNA components.  To utilize this technique in detecting respiratory pathogens, such as SARS-CoV-2, which is typically found in respiratory samples, we have designed a compact, affordable, and highly portable device: a digital PCR chip consisting of 1024 micro-reaction chambers and integrated fluidic systems for sample preparation, dPCR, and analysis.  The resulting device measures 18x16 cm, is fully automated from sample to data output, and can digitally detect COVID-19 in swab samples, even if the initial viral load is very low.  The experimental results confirm the reliability of this device's approach and its ability to accurately diagnose COVID-19 in swab samples with low viral loads.

certain non-terminating functions are difficult to define directly. To overcome this limitation, a clock mechanism is often introduced to enforce termination after a certain number of steps. After that point, the clock is reset to simplify reasoning about functions like infinite streams. However, resetting the clock breaks the original function's correctness due to its artificial termination limit. To resolve this dilemma, we propose using a specialized form of non-determinism to occasionally extend the steps allowed by the original function's termination bound, and only resetting the clock when this extended allowance is exhausted. This hybrid strategy enables us to define both the functions' correctness and termination in a natural and concise manner, while avoiding several difficulties associated with total functions and right-nondeterminism. To illustrate this method's advantages, we focus on defining infinite sequences of computations in total rewriting systems.

novel method to identify and categorize functional sites within proteins utilizing computer simulations. The primary objective behind developing this method stems from the substantial growth in experimental capacity over recent years and the subsequent increase in protein and peptide structure data available. The substantial data accumulation has led to a need for more accurate predictions of protein and peptide interactions, including how they bind, recognize each other, and demonstrate specificity. To address this requirement, our research team has developed a new approach utilizing computer simulations to uncover and categorize protein and peptide motifs that induce conformational specificity. The method involves the use of simulation techniques such as conformational sampling, analysis of motifs through clustering, and free energy calculations, ultimately enabling more precise predictions of protein and peptide behaviors in experimental settings. Furthermore, our method employs a machine learning approach to identify and categorize these functional sites, incorporating features derived from experimental and computational data, such as phylogenetic signals, three-dimensional protein coordinates, and biophysical characteristics. The method's effectiveness was validated through rigorous testing on numerous datasets, achieving high accuracy and specificity in identifying protein and peptide motifs that induce specificity in binding, surpassing traditional methods such as tree-based methods and deep learning methods. The outcomes of our research demonstrate the potential of our method in guiding further experimental investigations and shedding light on the mechanisms of conformational specificity, ultimately contributing to the understanding of protein and peptide behavior at a fundamental level.

imate near neighbor problem involves precomputing a data structure that efficiently finds nearest neighbors within a specified threshold. This problem enables applications like database search and machine learning tasks. This study tackles this problem in the high-dimensional Euclidean space. It introduces a new approach based on localized and expanded (LLE) versions of points and utilizes localized and expanded range search structures to develop an algorithm with specific time complexity and error margin properties. This results in a data structure with preprocessing and query time dependencies on dimensions d and threshold r, with corresponding error margins. Building on this data structure, a solution to the c-approximate near neighbor query problem is presented. This algorithm involves precomputing and query times with dimensions d and threshold r, resulting in a data structure with storage requirements and error margin properties. This research addresses the nearly optimal dependence on dimensionality d found in related work by Ahle et al. and establishes a new data structure with query time dependencies on dimensionality d and threshold r, with storage requirements and error margin properties. This research addresses the nearly optimal dependence on dimensionality d found in related work by Ahle et al. and establishes a lower bound on precomputation complexity in the pointer machine model of computation. measurement error correction (MEC) is a crucial technique. Our research introduces MEVC-19, a novel method that corrects individual qubit measurement errors in the IBM Quantum Eureka device by leveraging tailored classical-like states and demonstrated classical quantum correspondence. We validated that states with distinct quantum numbers are not easily affected by complex quantum fluctuations. Utilizing these coherent states, we identified and corrected errors in individual qubits, achieving an average improvement in measurement accuracy from 77.5% to 90.5%. Notably, our approach is significantly more straightforward and adaptable, capable of being extended to larger qubit arrays with minimal adjustments, unlike previous methods with more complex error rates that require additional classical calibration.

To achieve this effectively, robots need a way to account for potential errors that can accumulate, which is a challenge in the field of robotics. To address this issue, we developed the concept of a probabilistic landmarker - a new approach to landmark-based orientation that incorporates a probability distribution to represent uncertainty. In the concept of probler, we successfully demonstrate how this landmarker enables a robot to be accurately oriented even in cases of high uncertainty. Our landmarker inherently supports probabilistic mapping systems seamlessly, as the probability distribution representing the robot's state uncertainty is utilized during the orientation process. To ensure that the probability distribution representing uncertainty is accurately reflected, we developed an efficient, near-optimal path-finding algorithm specifically for probler. Our results show that probler successfully achieves the desired orientation targets in various environments under different initial state distributions, and it seamlessly integrates with probabilistic mapping systems in the Gmapping framework.

Health Records (EHR) has sparked significant interest in building robust models that can accurately predict long-term clinical outcomes. Nonetheless, the practicality of these models is hindered by issues related to data leakage and biased estimates, primarily due to unaddressed confounding factors and noisy univariate feature selection methods. To address these challenges, this research proposes a novel multi-feature approach, incorporating multiple predictive models, to identify effective treatments and dosages from EHR. Additionally, a statistical framework is introduced to account for missing not-at-random (MNAR) feature values in EHR. Experimental results demonstrate that this feature approach significantly surpasses previous models in predicting long-term clinical outcomes, specifically new onset atrial fibrillation and mortality after heart failure discharge.

process of data entry into electronic health records is crucial for improving clinical trial data quality and reducing bias in trial-end analyses. Developing an automated solution is particularly important for high-risk end-of-trial analyses. Although numerous machine learning approaches exist for data imputation, successfully implementing these models in diverse real-world settings can be challenging due to varying data structures and populations. In this context, we present ADAPTER (Adversarial Data Adaptation for Trial End Repurposing), a novel training architecture leveraging additional public data to facilitate data entry automation using natural language processing techniques. By utilizing pre-trained BERT models, ADAPTER generates synthetic data to enhance model performance in the target dataset. The synthetic data helps circumvent the typical challenges associated with learning from private data, where external data inadequately represents the target dataset. We evaluate ADAPTER using the IMPACT-AD study, a phase 4 trial assessing cariprazine in Parkinson's disease. The results indicate that ADAPTER successfully facilitates data entry automation in varying data structures and populations.

Federated statistical inference enables centralised model training, using distributed algorithms tailored for centralised processing, effectively overcoming limitations imposed by this heterogeneity. A novel class of federated inference methods can generate parameters consistent with the joint distribution of parameters across all edge devices, effectively addressing challenges posed by complex statistical models containing hidden variables. We propose an iterative algorithm to train probabilistic chart models in the context of federated inference, achieving convergence to stationary points under established conditions. We demonstrate this approach's efficacy in training energy consumption models for machine learning workloads on edge devices, effectively reducing transmission requirements to a single set of parameters, thus mitigating privacy concerns and minimizing communication overhead.

systems into machine learning models is physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). By integrating mathematical models with data-driven techniques, PINNs provide an alternative to traditional machine learning methods. However, most existing work on PINNs has focused on creating them from scratch using synthetic data. This study explores the feasibility and benefits of enhancing pre-trained PINNNs using real-world experimental data gathered from physical systems. We demonstrate that combining physics-informed loss terms with experimental data can lead to improved results compared to using either approach alone. Additionally, our research reveals that the performance of PINNNs varies significantly across different neural network architectures. Finally, we investigate transfer learning in PINNNs by training them on a source task and fine-tuning them on a new, related experimental dataset. Our findings suggest that by leveraging prior knowledge through PINNNs, we can achieve more accurate predictions on diverse physical systems with reduced data requirements.

The proposed framework offers significant improvements over existing air pollution modeling methodologies by incorporating high-resolution air pollution models.

Our objective is to determine the maximum size of such a hypergraph in terms of its number of vertices. Specifically, when k equals 1, this problem reduces to determining the maximum size of a family of uniform sets where each pair of sets is disjoint. We establish that for d >= 3, this value is O(n^{d-2 + 2/d}). Additionally, when k exceeds 1, this problem corresponds to determining the maximum size of a family of uniform sets where each pair of sets intersects in less than k+1 elements. We prove that this value is O(n), with the constant in the O(n) term depending on d and k.

To shed light on this problem, we conducted simulations and real-world experiments to analyze the behavior of spherical particles under the influence of gravity. By adjusting the gravity and fluid conditions, we were able to create a range of particle sedimentation speeds, from slow movements to rapid transitions out of the glassy state. We focused our study on how this gravity-induced sedimentation affects the properties of disordered and disordered particle systems. By studying particle vibrations and sound wave propagation, we discovered significant changes in the network of mechanical bonds and contact forces within the particle network as gravity increases. We discovered that the overall structure remains consistent, but the local contact patterns undergo substantial modifications. Furthermore, we found that the network of mechanical bonds and contact forces evolves in response to gravity-induced sedimentation. Notably, the changes in the network's stiffness align with those of a static, gravity-dominated particle network. By studying the gravity vs kinetic energy landscape, we were able to create a critical boundary that marks the end of vitrification and marks the beginning of particle clustering. This research provides valuable insights into the gravity vs kinetic energy landscape for spherical particles and contributes to a broader understanding of complex fluid dynamics.

This necessitates not only technical expertise, but also legal and ethical knowledge, and policy analysis skills. The cornerstone of our analysis lies within Germany's Road Traffic Act, specifically the portion detailing vehicle automation levels, while emphasizing Algorithmen-Transparenz (algorithmic transparency) as a key requirement under German legislation concerning vehicle automation. The European Commission's recommendation for vehicle automation transparency is reinterpreted as a critical imperative under German law, with implications for safety testing, data protection, and liability assessment in in-use scenarios. The incorporation of Algorithmen-Transparenz is seen as a valuable contribution of German legislation towards universal European standards, with implications for vehicle automation safety assessment in general.

soft-body dynamics play a significant role, particularly when it comes to controlling robots interacting with the environment in intricate ways. Currently, control software development often relies on a rigid approximation of these dynamics or neglects them entirely, leading to an increased reliance on trial-and-toil and diminished safety margins. To overcome this limitation, an open-source simulation tool known as MuJoCo has been introduced to accurately model soft-body dynamics in a highly efficient manner. By leveraging this simulation tool, research into the advancements of legged robotics can be significantly accelerated in terms of development speed, safety and cost. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of MuJoCo and demonstrates its effectiveness in handling soft-body dynamics, as well as its potential for assisting with model-based control techniques. A series of case studies involving quadruped robots manipulating objects and climbing inclined surfaces using soft grappling lines are presented to showcase these capabilities.

This gravity theory has been analyzed within the context of cosmology, particularly in relation to the acceleration of our universe. networks, the technology has evolved significantly from its initial IEEE 802.11 standard. A key aspect of this progression has been defining a layered approach, with each revision of IEEE 802.11 only specifying the physical layer for backward compatibility. This comprehensive method, employing detailed protocol specification and traceable design methods, has effectively addressed performance and capacity challenges in previous generations. However, it has proven difficult to apply to home LANs with diverse requirements and complex network environments. This disparity has led IEEE to introduce performance enhancements, such as IEEE 802.11be, in piecemeal fashion within each revision, increasing backend burdens and fragmenting performance enhancements. To overcome these challenges, a novel framework, called Distributed Requirement-Driven Framework (DRDF), is proposed to streamline development by decentralizing networking environments and streamlining downstream processing through a systematized process. This proposed framework has been evaluated and demonstrated to be a viable solution for meeting future next-generation home WiFi network requirements.
